title: Lent: forty days
hook: forty days of prayer, fasting and giving, echoing Jesus in the desert

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ash Wednesday, and your line: dust, and loved. The ash opens a season. Today, what comes next.

Every spring you hear it at work, at school, in group chats: so what are you giving up for Lent? Chocolate. Coffee. Social media. Swearing. One person gives up nothing and says they're giving up giving things up. It can sound like a second round of New Year's resolutions. But the season started somewhere much older and harder. In the Gospels, right after his baptism, Jesus goes out into the wilderness alone, and stays. The King James says, "And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he was afterward an hungred." Hungry, alone, tested, in the desert. Today's word is the season Christians built around those forty days.
screen: `WHAT ARE YOU GIVING UP?` → `INTO THE WILDERNESS.` → `FORTY DAYS AND FORTY NIGHTS.`

segments.voice: Lent. The English name is usually traced to an old word for spring, the season when the days lengthen. In Greek and Latin it's simply called the fortieth. Forty is a number the Bible keeps returning to: forty days of rain for Noah, forty days for Moses on the mountain, forty years for Israel in the wilderness, forty days for Elijah walking to the mountain of God, and forty days for Jesus in the desert. Readers hear forty as the Bible's number for a long, testing stretch that changes people. Lent is traditionally made of three practices, from Jesus's own teaching in the Sermon on the Mount: prayer, fasting and giving to the poor. He doesn't say if you fast. He says when. Churches keep it differently. Catholics fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, and abstain from meat on the Fridays of Lent. Orthodox Christians traditionally keep a fast without meat, dairy or eggs through Great Lent. Some Protestants choose something personal, or take something up instead: reading a Gospel, volunteering, calling someone each day. Some churches don't mark Lent at all. Underneath sits a shared idea: giving something up isn't a punishment. It's meant to make room. The hour you'd spend scrolling becomes an hour for prayer. The money you'd spend on coffee goes to someone who needs it. Some say the hunger itself reminds them what they're really hungry for. Christians call it a season of preparation, clearing space for Easter.
screen: `LENCTEN: SPRING.` · `FORTY: THE BIBLE'S TESTING NUMBER.` · `PRAYER, FASTING, GIVING.` · `LESS, TO MAKE ROOM.`

segments.voice: It doesn't have to be Lent right now: ask what's taking up too much room in your days, a habit, a screen, a snack, a complaint you keep repeating, and choose one small thing to set down for a week, or one to take up in its place. Keep it small enough that you'll actually do it. If you pray, you can offer it to God; if you don't, just notice what fills the space.
Lent. Forty days of prayer, fasting and giving before Easter, echoing Jesus in the desert. Today's word.
Your line: less, so there's room. Forty days, toward Easter. See you on day one hundred fifteen.
